reference.source: Rome Foundation criteria for functional anorectal disorders
clinicalPearls: Levator syndrome is a functional anorectal pain disorder characterised by chronic or recurrent dull, aching, or pressure-like pain high in the rectum, often described as sitting on a ball
It falls within the Rome classification of functional anorectal pain, distinguished from proctalgia fugax (brief fleeting episodes) by its longer duration, typically lasting twenty minutes or more
The defining physical sign is tenderness on posterior traction of the puborectalis during digital rectal examination, often more pronounced on the left
It is a diagnosis of exclusion, requiring the elimination of structural and inflammatory causes of anorectal pain such as abscess, fissure, thrombosis, malignancy, and coccygeal pathology
Pain is frequently worse with prolonged sitting and may be relieved by walking or lying down, and can be associated with pelvic-floor dysfunction and dyssynergic defecation
The Rome framework separates highly likely levator ani syndrome (with puborectalis tenderness) from unspecified functional anorectal pain (without it)
Management centres on reassurance, pelvic-floor physiotherapy and biofeedback, and adjuncts such as digital massage, warm baths, electrogalvanic stimulation, and muscle relaxation techniques
It commonly coexists with other functional gastrointestinal and pelvic-floor disorders and with psychological stressors, warranting a holistic approach
reference.pathophysiology: Levator syndrome is understood as a disorder of chronic spasm and tension in the pelvic-floor musculature, particularly the levator ani and puborectalis. Sustained or dysregulated contraction of these muscles, often in the setting of pelvic-floor dyssynergia, produces ischaemic, aching pain referred to the rectum and perineum. Central and peripheral sensitisation, abnormal pain processing, and the interplay of stress and anxiety contribute to symptom persistence, in keeping with a disorder of gut-brain and pelvic-floor interaction. There is no structural lesion; rather, heightened muscle tone, tenderness of the puborectalis, and impaired relaxation during defecation underlie the symptoms, which may be exacerbated by prolonged sitting and by dyssynergic straining.
additionalDifferentials: Coccygodynia or other musculoskeletal pelvic pain
Anal fissure, abscess, or thrombosed haemorrhoid
Chronic prostatitis or pelvic pain syndrome in men
additionalInvestigations: Digital rectal examination assessing puborectalis tenderness on posterior traction
Proctosigmoidoscopy to exclude mucosal or structural disease
Anorectal manometry and balloon expulsion to assess dyssynergia
Defecating proctography where obstructed defecation coexists
Pelvic MRI where structural, neurological, or gynaecological causes are suspected
Colonoscopy or cross-sectional imaging to exclude neoplasia in at-risk or alarm-symptom patients
redFlags: Rectal bleeding, weight loss, or a palpable mass suggesting malignancy
Fever or localised swelling suggesting abscess
Progressive neurological symptoms or saddle anaesthesia
New severe pain of abrupt onset with structural findings
Pain unresponsive to treatment with evolving alarm features
reference.prognosis: Levator syndrome is benign but often chronic and relapsing; a substantial proportion of patients improve with biofeedback, physiotherapy, and reassurance, though symptoms can persist and fluctuate, and response is generally better when puborectalis tenderness is present and pelvic-floor dyssynergia is addressed.
pitfalls: Diagnosing levator syndrome without adequately excluding structural or malignant causes
Overlooking coexisting dyssynergic defecation that is amenable to biofeedback
Attributing pain solely to haemorrhoids and performing unnecessary anal surgery
Neglecting the psychological and gut-brain dimension of the disorder
Repeated invasive investigations for a functional disorder once alarm features are excluded
references: Rome Foundation criteria for functional anorectal disorders
ASCRS Textbook of Colon and Rectal Surgery
Standard reference texts on functional gastrointestinal and pelvic-floor disorders
management: Reassurance and patient education about this functional anorectal pain disorder
Pelvic-floor physiotherapy and biofeedback targeting relaxation of the puborectalis
Digital massage of the levator muscles and warm baths for symptomatic relief
Electrogalvanic stimulation and neuromodulation for refractory symptoms
Muscle-relaxant strategies and treatment of coexisting dyssynergic defecation and constipation
Exclude structural and inflammatory anorectal causes, as it is a diagnosis of exclusion
Psychological support and stress management for the gut-brain component
